newsitem.title: GERMANY: Spain's king condemns ETA on visit to Germany.
newsitem.headline: Spain's king condemns ETA on visit to Germany.

text.p: King Juan Carlos of Spain on Wednesday strongly condemned the murder of a young town councillor by the Basque separatist group ETA, branding the guerrillas contemptible terrorists.
The king, on the first full day of a visit to Germany, also paid tribute to the slain politician, Miguel Angel Blanco.
"His murder was as contemptible as the terrorists who killed him," he told a reception in the Berlin city hall to welcome him to the German capital.
"We Spaniards are all in shock and I feel I must express my admiration for Miguel Angel as a person and for his life," said the king, who arrived in Berlin on Wednesday evening.
The king's language was stronger than comments he made during a rare televised address to the nation after Blanco's funeral on Monday.
In that speech, he said Blanco's death had not been in vain and praised the widespread reaction against the killing.

Blanco, a 29-year-old Basque town councillor and member of Spain's ruling party, was kidnapped last Thursday by ETA rebels who vowed to execute him in 48 hours if the government did not give in to their demands.
They shot him twice in the head on Saturday, and he died 12 hours later.

The killing of an ordinary, low-ranking official stunned Spaniards and marked a crucial turning point in public opinion. Basques who once whispered their opposition to ETA in private are now screaming it in public.
Berlin mayor Eberhard Diepgen thanked the king for going ahead with his visit, his first to Berlin since 1986, despite the difficult domestic situation.
"In the name of all Berliners, allow me to express our sympathies and concern in this difficult situation," he said.

"Berliners can feel with you and understand how the people of Spain are feeling," the mayor added. "Fighting terrorism is something that doesn't just affect one country. We too have our experience of that."

Juan Carlos and Queen Sofia were scheduled to take a city tour after the reception and walk through the Brandenburg Gate, a famous Berlin landmark that was closed off to the public during the Cold War because the Berlin Wall ran next to it.
"This visit to Berlin and the walk through the Brandenburg Gate symbolises the new Europe which has emerged in the last 10 years," Diepgen declared.
The king and queen are also scheduled to visit Bonn, Frankfurt and Dresden during their four-day stay in Germany.
